probe: nft runs and `nft -j list ruleset` parses; an empty ruleset is a successful read and an authoritative-empty commit, never a probe failure

collections.name: tailscale
collections.question: who is on the tailnet, and is this node's membership healthy?

HostName.sentence: The node's self-reported display name — free text in every sense, which is why it is a fact and never the row's identity: a stock Mac calls itself "Henry's MacBook Pro", with the space and the typographic apostrophe.

DNSName.sentence: The tailnet's own canonical machine name, whose first label is the row's identity — the name `tailscale status` itself prints.

TailscaleIPs.sentence: The node's tailnet addresses. NEVER a join key and never dialled from facts: the coordination server reassigns them on re-enrolment.

OS.sentence: The operating system the node reports.

Online.sentence: Whether the coordination map says the node is connected right now.

LastSeen.sentence: When the tailnet last saw this peer. Go stamps `never` as the year-one zero time, which is absence here — passed through raw it reads as two millennia of staleness (audit 2026-08-10).

Relay.sentence: The DERP relay the node is homed on, where one is.

CurAddr.sentence: The direct path in use to this peer. tailscale reports the empty string while relayed or idle, which is absence here: no direct path is a statement, not an empty address.

RxBytes.sentence: Bytes received from this peer since the daemon started.

TxBytes.sentence: Bytes sent to this peer since the daemon started.

ExitNode.sentence: Whether this peer is currently this node's exit node.

ExitNodeOption.sentence: Whether this node offers itself as an exit node.

KeyExpiry.sentence: When this node's key expires, normalised to seconds UTC. A tagged node's key does not expire: the field is absent or Go's zero time, and either way this is absent — never a verdict.

KeyExpiryDays.sentence: Whole days until the key expires, computed at collect so the expiry rule stays clockless. Negative once expired.

BackendState.sentence: The daemon's own state word — Running is the healthy one. Only the self row carries it, which is what keeps the offline rule from judging peers: whether a PEER should be online is expected-state territory, not this collection's.

Health.sentence: The daemon's own health messages, verbatim, present only when it says something. tailscaled uses these for advisories too, which is why their presence informs rather than warns — the messages themselves are the substance.

PrimaryRoutes.sentence: The subnet routes this node is primary for. If the advertisement lapses the fact disappears — exactly the goes-dark change an expected-state check needs to see (audit 2026-08-10).

TailscaleSnapshotAt.sentence: When the root collector wrote the snapshot these facts came from — the SMART contract exactly: the facts are only as fresh as the file.

TailscaleSnapshotAgeSeconds.sentence: How old the snapshot is right now, computed at collect so the staleness rule stays pure.

rules.sentence: The node key expires within a week, or has expired.
The node key expires within a month.
The node is not connected to the tailnet.
The daemon reports health messages; they are the substance, and they are on the row.
These tailscale facts are last-known, not current: the snapshot is stale, so the collector may be wedged or not running on this host.

collections.redaction_exemption: the tailnet names, addresses, relays and routes are declared location or content fact by fact and handled by disclosure policy — the corpus stages a crafted snapshot, so nothing here is a real tailnet's identity. Counters, states and booleans are the daemon's own vocabulary; no key material of any kind appears in `tailscale status` output.

reference_commands.purpose: the snapshot this collection reads, as the collector takes it

collections.name: port-exposure
collections.question: which firewall rules admit each listening port, and from where?

Protocol.sentence: The listening socket's protocol, joined from the listening collection.

LocalAddress.sentence: The address the socket is bound to; the wildcard means the ruleset alone decides what reaches it.

LocalPort.sentence: The port this row is about — the number an operator arrives asking after, which is why it is the row rather than a column on a rule.

Scope.sentence: What the binding says before any rule: a loopback socket is unreachable from off the host whatever the ruleset permits.

AdmittingRules.sentence: Every rule on the input path that admits this port, in evaluation order, each with its handle and rendered text. Evidence for the two answers below, and the thing to go and read.

AdmittedFromCertain.sentence: The source constraints of admitting rules that were rendered in full — where traffic can reach this port from, by rules this observer understood completely. A clause it could not read contributes nothing here, so this is a lower bound and can only ever under-claim.

AdmittedFromPossible.sentence: The same computation with every unreadable clause treated as matching — an upper bound. Where this is wider than the certain answer, the difference is the part of the ruleset this observer cannot interpret rather than a property of the firewall.

ClosureGap.sentence: Whether the two answers differ. True means the ruleset contains a clause this adapter could not read that bears on this port, and the rules responsible are named beside it.

ClosureGapRules.sentence: The handles of the rules whose unreadable clauses opened the gap — where to look to close it by hand.

PathCoverage.sentence: Which packet paths this row accounts for. Input only: a published container port is translated in prerouting and admitted in forward and is not covered, so an empty admitting list is not a statement that nothing can reach the port. Stated on every row rather than once, because a consumer holding one object must be able to see it. Shadowing is not resolved and connection tracking is not modelled: rules are listed in evaluation order, and an earlier drop that would pre-empt a later accept is shown rather than applied.

collections.redaction_exemption: addresses a socket is bound to and rendered rule text — interface names, subnets and ports somebody chose, declared location and content above; the corpus scrub substitutes them. No credential appears in a ruleset this collection can render, and a rule comment is not read at all.

reference_commands.purpose: the sockets these rows join, by hand
the input-path rules the closures walk

collections.name: nft-tables
collections.question: which firewall tables exist, and how much does each hold?

Family.sentence: The address family this table filters. The same table name in ip and ip6 is two tables, which is why the family is in the row's own name.

Chains.sentence: The table's chains by name, each with its policy where one is declared, in the ruleset's own order. Chain names are words somebody chose.

ChainCount.sentence: How many chains the table holds.

RuleCount.sentence: How many rules the table holds — COUNTED, never read. No fact on this row says what any rule matches or permits, so a ruleset that admits one port from one interface and one that admits everything are indistinguishable here: deleting the single rule that admits sshd moves this from 25 to 24 and changes nothing else on this page. The rules themselves are the nft-rules collection and this collection's evidence.

collections.redaction_exemption: a family, a count, and a list of chain names with their policies. Table and chain names are distribution conventions or operator-chosen words and are declared content; no rule body and no comment is read by this collection at all.

reference_commands.purpose: the tables this collection rows, by hand
the full ruleset — every match, port, interface and verdict these rows deliberately do not read

collections.name: nft-chains
collections.question: where does the kernel enter this ruleset, and what runs what?

Family.sentence: The address family this chain's table belongs to — ip, ip6, inet, arp, bridge or netdev. The same chain name in ip and ip6 is two chains, and a rule admitting a port in one says nothing about the other.

Table.sentence: The table holding this chain. On a real host the table name is an ownership label: docker, libvirt, firewalld and nixos-fw were each written by something different.

Name.sentence: The chain's name, as its author wrote it.

Handle.sentence: The kernel's own identifier for this chain object.

BaseChain.sentence: Whether the kernel calls this chain directly. A base chain is registered against a hook and every packet on that path enters it; a regular chain runs only when something jumps to it, which is why the two need telling apart before any rule in either is read.

Hook.sentence: The netfilter hook this base chain is registered against — prerouting, input, forward, output or postrouting. It is WHERE in the packet's journey this chain runs, and absent on a regular chain because nothing calls it directly.

Type.sentence: What the kernel lets this base chain do: filter chains decide, nat chains translate, route chains can re-run the routing decision. Absent on a regular chain.

Priority.sentence: The order this base chain runs in relative to others on the same hook, lowest first. Two chains on one hook are both traversed; this says which sees the packet first, and a negative number is normal.

Policy.sentence: What happens to a packet that reaches the end of this base chain matching nothing — accept or drop. It is the verdict the whole chain falls back to, so a chain of narrow accepts under an accept policy admits everything the rules did not mention. Absent on a regular chain, which returns to its caller instead.

RuleCount.sentence: How many rules this chain holds. Counted, never read: this says nothing about what any of them permits.

JumpedFrom.sentence: Every chain that transfers control here, by jump or goto — how a packet reaches this chain at all. Derived by reading every rule's target across the whole ruleset, and the elements of every named verdict map some rule uses, so it is the answer to 'what runs this' that no single chain's own document contains.

Unreferenced.sentence: Stated only when true, and only for a regular chain: no rule, and no named verdict map any rule uses, jumps or gotos here, and the kernel does not call it, so no packet can reach any rule in it. Usually a leftover; occasionally a rule that was meant to be reachable and is not.

collections.redaction_exemption: every served fact is a chain's own structural member — family, table, chain name, handle, hook, type, priority, policy — or a count or caller list derived from them. Table and chain names are distribution conventions, the rest are protocol constants, and no rule body and no comment is read by this collection at all.

reference_commands.purpose: the chains this collection rows, by hand
the same ruleset with chain handles and hooks

collections.name: nft-rules
collections.question: what does each rule in this ruleset actually say?

Family.sentence: The address family this rule's table belongs to — ip, ip6, inet, arp, bridge or netdev.

Table.sentence: The table holding this rule. On a real host the table name is an ownership label: docker, libvirt, firewalld and nixos-fw were each written by something different, and this observer sees all of them at once where a manager's own UI sees only its own.

Handle.sentence: The kernel's own identifier for this rule, and the join key to `nft -a list ruleset`. Stable while the rule object lives; a flush-and-restore reassigns handles, so it is not durable across a reload.

Position.sentence: This rule's ordinal within its chain. Evaluation is ordered and first-match-wins, so position is meaning, not presentation.

Rendered.sentence: What this rule says, in nft's own vocabulary, with every term present. A term whose meaning could not be expanded appears at its position as a placeholder rather than being dropped — omission would turn a narrow rule into a permissive-looking one.

Verdict.sentence: How this rule ends — accept, drop, reject, return, continue or queue — or absent where the rule ends in no verdict at all, which is what a pure counter or logging rule does.

JumpTarget.sentence: The chain this rule transfers control to. A jump is not a decision: what happens is decided by the chain it goes to.

Comprehension.sentence: How much of this rule the renderer could state: full where every statement was rendered, partial where some were not, opaque where the rule's conditions are absent from the source document entirely. Computed by subtracting what the renderer consumed from the rule's own expression list, never assumed.

OpaqueReason.sentence: Why a rule's conditions could not be read: xt where it calls an xtables extension whose parameters nft's JSON does not carry, text-fallback where nft emitted a bare string because it had no JSON encoder for the expression.

Residue.sentence: The expressions in this rule the renderer did not consume, verbatim. This is the measured extent of what the row above does not say.

CounterPackets.sentence: Packets this rule has matched, where the rule carries a counter. nftables has no implicit per-rule counters, so absence here means the rule was written without one — never that nothing has matched.

CounterBytes.sentence: Bytes this rule has matched, where the rule carries a counter. Absent means no counter was written, not zero traffic.

Handle.sentence: The handle of the rule that transfers control, which is what tells apart several jumps from one chain to the same target. Position would not: deleting a rule above renumbers every rule below it, and a discriminator that moves is a key that resets a relation's lifecycle for a change it had nothing to do with.

reference_commands.purpose: the same rules with '# handle N', as nft prints them
the document this collection reads
renders the xt rules this collection cannot

collections.name: routes
collections.question: where does this host send traffic, in every table the kernel consults — and does anything outrank its own connected routes?

Destination.sentence: The prefix this route matches, or `default`. An address by construction, which is why this whole collection's address facts are classed as location.

Gateway.sentence: The next hop, where the route has one — a directly connected route does not, and says so by this fact's absence.

Protocol.sentence: Who installed the route, in iproute2's word — kernel, dhcp, static, bird.

Scope.sentence: The route's scope; `link` in main is the definition of being directly attached to a segment.

PrefSrc.sentence: The source address the kernel prefers for traffic using this route.

Metric.sentence: The route's metric, deciding between same-prefix routes within one table.

Family.sentence: Which stack the route belongs to, read off the destination itself so the label cannot contradict the address beside it; only `default` carries no address and keeps its dump's family.

Table.sentence: The routing table holding this route. iproute2 omits it for main; naming it beats an absence a reader has to know the default of.

RulePreference.sentence: The lowest rule preference selecting this table — what decides whether it outranks main, which sits at 32766 unless something moves it. Absent when no rule names the table.

ShadowsLocalPrefix.sentence: An exact structural comparison, not a judgement: this route is in a table the kernel consults before main, and main holds a kernel-scope link route for the same destination — the shape that took a site LAN down twice while every screen showed a healthy main table. Present only when true.

rules.sentence: A policy table consulted ahead of main carries a route for a segment this host is directly attached to: replies to LAN neighbours go into the tunnel while ARP keeps answering, and the host looks half-alive. Warn, not critical — on a deliberate split tunnel this is exactly what was intended.

collections.redaction_exemption: every address fact is declared location and handled by disclosure policy; the rest are kernel routing metadata with no credential surface

reference_commands.purpose: both families, every table
and the v6 half
the rule preferences that decide which table wins

collections.name: listening
collections.question: what is this host accepting traffic on, and from how far away can it be reached?

Protocol.sentence: Which socket table the row came from.

LocalAddress.sentence: The address the socket is bound to, decoded word-wise from /proc/net's host-order hex — the encoding that read backwards produces plausible wrong addresses.

LocalPort.sentence: The bound port — the number an operator scans for, and this collection's applied order leads with it.

Uid.sentence: The owning uid, from /proc/net itself — what can be said about the process without the privilege to name it.

SocketInode.sentence: The socket's inode, the join key a privileged reader would use to name the process.

Scope.sentence: What the binding says about reach: a wildcard socket is reachable from wherever the ruleset allows, a loopback one from nowhere off the host whatever the ruleset says.

ProcessUnobservable.sentence: Why the listening process is not named on this row — stated on every row rather than once on the collection, so a consumer reading one object does not need the source block to know.

TablesUnreadable.sentence: Which /proc/net tables would not open, when any would not: a table that cannot be read is not a table with nothing in it, and without this a host whose udp6 was unreadable would publish a complete-looking list of TCP sockets.

collections.redaction_exemption: bound addresses are declared location and handled by disclosure policy; ports, uids and inodes are kernel socket metadata with no credential surface

reference_commands.purpose: the same tables, by hand
the friendly rendering most operators know

collections.name: resolver
collections.question: which mechanism answers this host's lookups, and where do they actually go?

ResolverService.sentence: Which mechanism is speaking: systemd-resolved over the bus, or the file glibc reads. The question is universal and only the answer is not — a dhcpcd-written resolv.conf is still a resolver.

Nameservers.sentence: File mode: every nameserver line, in file order — all of them, though glibc uses only the first three.

SearchDomains.sentence: The search list. In file mode a later search or domain line REPLACES an earlier one, glibc's own surprising rule, kept faithfully; in resolve1 mode the configured domains, route-only ones marked.

Options.sentence: File mode: resolver options, accumulated across lines as glibc accumulates them.

ResolvConfTarget.sentence: Where /etc/resolv.conf points when it is a symlink — usually the name of whoever manages the file.

CurrentDNSServer.sentence: resolve1's manager-level current server. Sticky across the boot window; the per-link map is where ordinary queries actually go, which is what this collection exists to make readable.

DNSServersInUse.sentence: The union of everything configured, globally or on any link — the answer to 'who does this host ask'.

GlobalDNSServers.sentence: System-scope servers: classic global scope, plus servers homed on loopback — a deliberate local recursive resolver is system-scope by construction, the measured systemd-261 behaviour that once fired a false warn.

PerLinkDNS.sentence: Per-link resolver state, where DHCP-provided DNS actually lives: each link's servers, its current pick, its domains, and whether it takes the DNS default route — the member that decides where ordinary queries go.

FallbackDNSServers.sentence: The compiled-in fallbacks resolved would use with nothing configured — public resolvers the operator never chose, which is exactly why the fallback rule exists.

ResolvConfMode.sentence: How resolved is managing /etc/resolv.conf, in its own word — stub, static, foreign.

NoLinkTakesDNSDefaultRoute.sentence: Derived so the fallback judgement can be rule-table data: true when the per-link walk observed DefaultRoute on every link that has servers and none carries it. Absent where any link could not say — cannot-see is not 'no'.

rules.sentence: No DNS server is configured anywhere this host's resolver looks; lookups fall to whatever answers on localhost, which on most hosts is nothing.

No link takes the DNS default route and no global servers are configured, so every query outside the configured domains goes to the compiled-in public fallback servers — resolvers the operator never chose.

collections.redaction_exemption: every server and domain fact is declared location and handled by disclosure policy; the mode strings are resolved's own closed vocabulary

reference_commands.purpose: the resolve1 view, where resolved runs
the file glibc reads, everywhere
the exact manager document this collector parses

collections.name: links
collections.question: what interfaces does this host have, what is each one really, and is anything that should carry traffic down?

OperState.sentence: The kernel's operational state, lowered — up is the only positively healthy word; lo, wireguard and tun report unknown because they have no carrier to detect, which is why the quiet states are not judged.

Kind.sentence: The kernel's most specific name for what this SOFTWARE device is — bridge, veth, tun, tap, with tun/tap split one level down in linkinfo because one driver creates both. Absent on every physical interface and loopback: that absence is the statement 'not a software device', and LinkType is what names those.

LinkType.sentence: The kernel's hardware type (ARPHRD), present on everything: ether, loopback, or none for a layer-3 tunnel with no link-layer header at all — which is also why such a device has no MAC. Not a physical/virtual discriminator: a bridge is ether too.

MACAddress.sentence: The address in use — the join key the bridge fdb and a container runtime both speak, declared as the identity it is.

PermanentMACAddress.sentence: The address burned into the hardware, carried only when it differs from the one in use — the tell that a MAC has been overridden, which otherwise takes a reader to the machine to discover.

Master.sentence: The bridge or bond this link is enslaved to. The same statement travels as the enslaved-to relation, which is what the tree derives from.

Addresses.sentence: Every address configured on the link, with its prefix length — and the fact the down-but-configured judgement reads: a down link carrying addresses is something that should be working.

ParentBus.sentence: The bus behind the device, present only where there is hardware — pci on a real NIC, virtio on a VM's, exactly the distinction a synthesised physical flag would have destroyed.

ParentDev.sentence: The bus address, kept exactly as the kernel spells it: the join key to the hardware collections.

BridgeMembers.sentence: How many links are enslaved to this bridge, carried on bridges only: zero is the empty-bridge rule's whole condition, because the kernel only raises a bridge when a member is up.

PeerMACAddresses.sentence: The MACs the bridge has learned behind this port — what makes a veth attributable to its container, since the port's own MAC identifies nothing. Learned and aging: absence is silence, never evidence that nothing is attached.

LLDPNeighbors.sentence: What the far end of the wire says it is, where anything on the segment emits LLDP: system name, port, chassis id — the facts a neighbour resolution joins on.

rules.sentence: Bridge is down with no member ports — an empty bridge is down by design; its address is daemon-assigned, not intent.
Link is administratively present but not up, and it carries configured addresses — something that should be working is not.
Link is administratively present but not up, with nothing configured on it — inventory, not trouble: an unwired spare NIC or an unused radio.

collections.redaction_exemption: addresses and LLDP neighbour facts are declared location, the MAC family identity, each handled by disclosure policy; the rest is kernel link metadata

reference_commands.purpose: the same tree, by hand
the learned MACs behind each bridge port
the far ends of the wires, where LLDP speaks
